fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on which kind of increase we're talking about. Because there are two things that get conflated. One is the kind of capability that shows up on evals, where the model gets better at a benchmark, and the other is the kind that actually changes what people do day to day. And right now those two have diverged quite a bit. The models are very impressive on the evals, and then you put them into some real workflow and it's... it's weird. It's jagged. It does something brilliant and then it makes a mistake that a person would never make, and you have to go in and fix it.

So in the near term, I expect the effect to be more incremental than people think. People will use these tools, they'll get some productivity, companies will restructure a bit around them. But the thing that really changes how things are done is when the models can learn on the job. When you can deploy one and it gets better from being deployed, the way a person does. A person who starts a job is not that useful on day one, and then six months later they're very useful, and it's not because they read more books. It's because they went through the experience. Our models don't really do that yet.

And when that gets solved, and I think it will get solved, then it stops being gradual. Because then the thing you've deployed is not a tool anymore, it's more like a worker, or a lot of workers, who all learn and who can share what they learn. At that point the rate at which things change becomes something that we don't really have good intuitions for. All the economic growth we've seen was constrained by how fast humans can learn and how many of them there are. Remove that constraint and the question of how things are done becomes... I think much more a question of what we decide to do with it than what's technically possible. And that's the part I actually spend more time thinking about.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's very hard to imagine, and I think that's actually the central difficulty. Right now, when people talk about AI, even people who work on it, it still feels kind of abstract. You read that the models can do this or that, there are announcements, but in your day-to-day life it doesn't really feel that different. And I think there's a real gap between how impressive these models look on evaluations and how much they've actually changed the economy. That gap is itself a very interesting thing that tells you something about what's still missing.

But I expect that as the capabilities increase, that abstraction will go away. AI will become something people actually feel. And once that happens, I think a lot of behavior will change in ways that are hard to predict from where we sit today. Companies will behave differently. I think the frontier companies will become much more concerned about safety, in a very concrete way, once they see the power with their own eyes. Governments will want to do things. The public will want things to be done. Today it's hard to get people to take it seriously because it's hard to imagine. When it's right in front of you, it's not hard to imagine anymore.

Then there's the economic side. Once you have a system that can learn to do any job, the way a person can learn, and you have many copies of it, and those copies can share what they've learned, I think you get very rapid economic growth, at least in some places. How rapid is genuinely uncertain, because the world is big and things have inertia, and different countries will make different choices about what to allow. But I think it will be quite dramatic.

And I'd say one more thing. A lot of how things are done today rests on the assumption that intelligence is scarce: you need to hire people, train them, wait for them to get good. If that assumption stops being true, a great many institutions will need to rethink themselves. Exactly how that plays out, I don't think anyone really knows yet.

fable-5.text:
You know, it's a big question, and I think the honest answer is that it will happen more gradually than people expect at first, and then more dramatically than people expect later.

Right now, we are in a stage where AI is very impressive in evals, very impressive in demonstrations, and yet its economic impact is noticeably lagging behind. The models can do these amazing things, and yet when you look at how the economy actually runs, how companies actually operate, things are still mostly done by people in mostly the same way as before. There is this gap, and I think the gap exists because the models, as capable as they are, still have this jaggedness — they are superhuman in some ways and surprisingly unreliable in others. They don't generalize the way a person does. A person can be taught something once and they get it; the model needs a lot more, and it can make strange mistakes that a competent person would never make.

But the thing to keep in mind is that this is not a permanent condition. As the capabilities increase — and in particular, as the models become genuinely reliable, as they learn to learn the way people learn — then the way things are done changes very fundamentally. Because at that point, you're not talking about a tool that helps a person do their work. You're talking about something that can do the work. And when the AI can do the work, including the work of doing AI research itself, then you get this loop where capabilities increase even faster, and the economy starts to be able to grow in ways that were just not possible before, because the bottleneck of skilled human labor is removed.

So my expectation is something like this: a period that feels slower than the hype, where the AI is diffusing into companies and workflows and people are figuring out how to use it, and then a transition into something that is genuinely very fast and very different. And I think one of the most important things — maybe the most important thing — is that during that second phase, the AI itself, and the people building it, need to care about getting it right. Because once things are done by AI rather than by people, the question of what the AI is trying to do becomes the whole question.

opus-5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's going to be strange, and strange in a way that's hard to see from the inside.

Right now the dominant mode is assistance. There's a person who has a job, the AI makes that person faster at parts of the job, and the job is still the job. The shape of the work doesn't change. And I think that's why the economic impact, so far, looks real but modest — you're putting a very powerful thing into a slot that was designed for a much smaller thing.

What changes as capability increases is that at some point the model isn't making the person faster at a task, it's doing the task. And then a sequence of tasks. And then you have to ask what the person is actually for. I think for quite a while the answer is judgment and responsibility — you want someone the thing answers to, someone who notices when the model is confidently wrong in a way the model itself cannot notice. That's a real job, but it's a different job, and there are fewer of them.

The thing I'd emphasize is that the bottleneck is not where people think it is. If you look at these models, their performance on evals is spectacular and their reliability over long horizons is not. A human who's been at a job for six months has absorbed something about that job that we don't know how to give a model yet. People get better by doing the work; the models mostly don't, not yet. So I expect a period where the capability is clearly there and the integration is clearly lagging, and people will disagree about whether that gap is a fundamental limitation or just engineering. I think it's mostly a research problem, and research problems get solved.

And then past that — if you actually take seriously that these systems will be able to do everything we can do, the question of how things are done stops being a question about workflows. It becomes a question of what we want, and who decides. Which is not a technical question. I think that transition is going to be harder than the endpoint, and we spend much less time thinking about it.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer starts with how hard this is to imagine. Right now AI is still abstract for most people. They read about it, they play with a chatbot, but it hasn't changed how they work or how institutions run. I expect that to change as the capabilities become more tangible. When you can see a system do something that clearly matters, that's when behavior shifts.

The first effect will be very practical. Work that used to take a lot of people and a lot of time will take far fewer of both. That will happen across many fields at once, and the speed will be surprising. It won't feel like a gradual improvement. Something will go from "interesting" to "obviously useful" very quickly, and people and companies will reorganize around it.

The second effect is on the AI companies, governments, and everyone else. People tend to behave differently once they feel the power of something. I think companies that are fierce competitors today will become more willing to collaborate on safety. Governments and the public will care much more about what's happening. And the people building the technology will become more serious about it, because it's much easier to be casual about something you can't feel yet.

So I'd put it in two parts. There's the economic and practical transformation, which will be big. And there's a change in how everyone relates to the technology once it's real to them. The second part may matter more, because it determines whether we handle the first part well.

I'd also say that I'm uncertain about the details. I'm fairly confident about the direction. I'm much less confident about what the world looks like when it's all deployed, because the thing we're trying to reason about is so different from anything we've dealt with before.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the biggest change is in what counts as a unit of work. Today we mostly use these systems as faster versions of things we already do: draft this, answer that, look this up. As capabilities grow, a person will be able to hand over a whole task, have a system work on it for hours or days, check its own output, and come back with a result. The person's job shifts toward directing that work and judging whether it's good.

I think that changes how companies and research operate too. When trying an idea gets cheap, you can explore far more of them, and the bottleneck moves from execution to taste: deciding which problems are worth solving and recognizing when an answer is actually right. People who are good at asking the right questions will become much more valuable.

It won't be even, though, and it will be disorienting. Some domains will absorb this quickly. Others will move slowly because feedback is slow or the stakes are high. A lot of the difficulty isn't technical. Institutions and people's sense of what their work is for have to adjust, and that may need to happen faster than they're used to.

So I don't expect one moment where everything changes. I expect a gradual shift in what gets delegated, until handing work to these systems is the default rather than the exception. Getting that transition right is one of the more important things we'll have to figure out.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot depends on what, exactly, the AI can do reliably. There’s a difference between an AI that can give you a useful answer and an AI that you can give a project to, and it will go and do the project. As you move from the first to the second, the implications become much larger.

At first, you use it to help with the way you already do things. But eventually you start asking: why are we doing things this way at all? If some kind of intellectual work becomes very inexpensive, you can try many more approaches. You can investigate things that wouldn’t have been worth investigating before.

Scientific research is a particularly interesting example, because progress there changes what else is possible. But I would be cautious about predicting the exact sequence. Even if the capabilities advance quickly, it takes time for people to understand them, trust them, and reorganize around them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on how far the capabilities go. If you have a system that can do some part of your job, then you use it as a tool. You still decide what to do, you give it a task, you check the result. Things become faster, but the way you work is still recognizable.

As the systems become more capable, that can change. You might be able to give a system an entire project, including figuring out which problems need to be solved. Then you have to ask: how should work be organized when that is possible? And if these systems can also do research, they can change the technology available to us, which creates another layer of change.

So I would expect very substantial effects. But I’m less confident about the specific sequence. There’s a difference between a system being able to do something and people figuring out how to use that ability reliably.

sol-6.text: I think the biggest change is that more and more tasks will become collaborations between people and AI systems. At first, the systems help with pieces of a job—writing code, analyzing information, generating ideas. As they become more capable, they may take on longer chains of reasoning and help solve problems that currently require entire teams. That could change the pace of scientific research and how organizations work. But the more responsibility we give these systems, the more important it becomes to understand their behavior and make sure they do what we actually intend.

terra-5.6.text: I think it will change almost everything. As these systems become more capable, they’ll increasingly be able to do intellectual work alongside people—and eventually much of it independently. That has enormous potential to make us more productive and accelerate scientific progress, but it also means we need to be very deliberate about how we manage the risks.

sol-5.6.text: As capabilities increase, more and more of the work that people do will be done by AI. At first it will be a tool that helps you think and act more effectively, but eventually it will become capable of carrying out entire projects—perhaps even doing AI research itself. At that point, the way companies, science, and society operate will change very dramatically.

luna-5.6.text: I think the main effect will be that intelligence becomes much more abundant and inexpensive. At first, AI will be used as a tool to help people do their existing jobs—writing, coding, research, analysis—but as the systems become more capable, they’ll increasingly perform entire tasks and eventually entire occupations. Organizations will be redesigned around having large numbers of very capable digital workers. Science and engineering could accelerate dramatically, because you’ll have systems that can help formulate hypotheses, run experiments, and solve difficult technical problems. The consequences will be enormous, and probably much faster than most people expect, because each improvement in AI can also help us improve AI itself.”

luna-6.text: I think it will change a lot of things, because intelligence is involved in so much of what people do. As these systems get more capable, they’ll take on more of the work people currently do themselves, and they’ll also help people do things that are difficult or impossible today. The details will depend on how quickly we build and deploy them, but I expect the overall effect to be very large.
